problem: Image-goal navigation methods (end-to-end RL, topological graphs, BEV-map memory such as RNR-Map) cannot model the 3D geometric relation between the explored scene and the goal image, and BEV-based memory forces the goal image to be horizontal and taken by the agent's own camera. Using 3DGS directly is too slow (optimization) and the 6-DoF pose search space is too large.
motivation: Image-goal navigation needs low-level visual features (texture, colour) and precise 3D alignment, which topological or semantic memories lose. An explicit, renderable 3D representation could preserve these and support goal images taken by arbitrary cameras (e.g. a cellphone), which matters for real deployment.
key_idea: Incrementally build a 3DGS map with a feed-forward monocular RGB-D predictor, coarsely localize the goal via 5-D pose matching implemented as a 3D convolution over voxelized scene features, then refine the pose by differentiable rendering with LoFTR matching constraints.
insight: Turning the 5-D (x,y,z,θ,φ) pose search into a single 3D convolution, with goal embeddings rotated over an icosahedral sphere as kernels, makes coarse localization real-time. Ablations show the subdivision level matters (level 1→3: SR 19.7→57.0 narrow FOV) and the 3DGS-based stopper plus matching-constrained optimization beat both no stopper (45.7 SR) and SLING (49.0 SR). Optimizing only confidently matched pairs in 3D compensates for the degraded quality of the unoptimized incremental 3DGS.
method: Incremental 3DGS: a UNet encoder plus Gaussian head predicts pixel-aligned Gaussians (position residuals, opacity, covariance, SH) from each RGB-D frame; Gaussians and 3D embeddings are unioned over time and pruned by opacity and density.

Free-view pose space: camera rotation is parameterized by two angles (θ,φ), since the phone/camera top edge stays parallel to the ground. Together with (x,y,z) this gives a 5-D space, with rotations discretized by γ-level icosahedron subdivision into N vertices.

Coarse localization via 3D convolution: scene embeddings are voxelized (pillar-based) and the N rotated goal embeddings, quantized to L^3 voxels, serve as N convolution kernels, with MLPs f1/f2 aligning the feature spaces. The argmax of the X×Y×Z×N activation map gives the coarse pose. Training uses focal loss plus cross-entropy on offline video.
Exploration policy: the activation map is projected to BEV and thresholded by σ_a. The agent goes to its maximum, otherwise to the nearest frontier on an occupancy map, planning with FMM.

Rendering-based stopper: render the current view with the goal camera's intrinsics and run LoFTR against the goal image. If the match count exceeds τ, the goal is deemed in view and fine localization starts.

Matching-constrained fine localization: optimize the SE(3) pose by minimizing the mean 3D distance between LoFTR-matched, depth-lifted points of the goal and the rendered image (backpropagated through rendered color and depth). The XY of the result becomes the FMM goal.
Missing depth/intrinsics of the goal image are estimated with UniDepth; the feed-forward model is trained with L2+LPIPS on novel-view rendering.

setting.backbone: Custom UNet encoder + Gaussian head (feed-forward 3DGS), 3D-conv coarse localizer trained from scratch; frozen LoFTR and UniDepth; FMM planner
setting.training_data: Passive offline RGB-D video episodes sampled from the Gibson image-goal navigation training set (72 houses); free-view variant trained on collected free-view Gibson data
setting.observation: Posed egocentric RGB-D stream (depth, intrinsics and pose given) plus goal image; no GPS/compass beyond pose
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level: move_forward, turn_left, turn_right, stop (via FMM on BEV map)
setting.privileged: Posed RGB-D (GT pose) and depth/intrinsics of the goal image (or UniDepth-estimated in an ablation)

numbers_note: Split for the Gibson image-goal results is inferred as val-unseen (14 validation houses in the NRNS dataset). The free-view benchmark is the authors' own Gibson-based set, labelled 'val' here. Per-difficulty breakdowns exist in the tables but only overall numbers are listed.
results: On the NRNS Gibson image-goal benchmark IGL-Nav reaches 76.8/64.1 SR/SPL (straight) and 73.5/62.4 (curved), beating the strongest baselines RNR-Map (68.2 SR straight, 65.7 SR curved) and FeudalNav (55.5 SPL straight). On the harder free-view setting it reaches 57.0/48.2 (narrow FOV) and 63.3/55.0 (wide FOV) SR/SPL supervised versus 32.4/21.8 and 37.4/26.0 for NRNS+SLING; even zero-shot transfer (43.1 and 47.4 SR) beats the supervised baselines.
limitations: Requires depth and camera intrinsics of the goal image (estimated with UniDepth, which costs 3-3.5 SR points) and posed RGB-D observations.
Coarse localization cost grows with the subdivision level γ, limiting angular resolution and making training inefficient.
Real-world evaluation is qualitative only (no quantitative real-robot results); the incremental 3DGS is unoptimized, so its quality degrades.
